Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma, the combination of threat items is not fully coherent: startle response and physical reactivity fit PTSD, but risky behavior is a different symptom style and is weakly connected to the rest of this profile. With only Threat and Memory represented, risky behavior lacks support from the other selected items and does not read as a clear trauma-linked threat perception.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: Within Memory, the items suggest overwhelmed, poorly verbalized traumatic recall, which is coherent for PTSD. However, intense guilt on recall introduces a strong negative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent from the profile. Given the formulation only shows a Threat → Memory link and no active Negative Appraisals connections, this item is not well aligned with the stated cognitive pattern.

vignette:
David, a 46-year-old African American man, sought therapy after a year of increasing distress following a traumatic encounter with law enforcement. A year prior, while driving home late from his job as a curriculum designer, he had been pulled over for what he felt was an ambiguous traffic violation. The interaction quickly escalated; two officers, one particularly aggressive, had shouted at him, ordered him out of his vehicle, and frisked him roughly on the roadside, all while accusing him of resisting. He remembered the blinding glare of the police cruiser's headlights, the chilling bark of commands, and the profound, gut-wrenching terror of being utterly powerless and vulnerable under the night sky.

In the months that followed, David found himself increasingly trapped by a pervasive sense of dread. He developed a pronounced startle response, jumping violently at unexpected noises, whether it was a colleague dropping a pen in the quiet office or the sudden ring of his mobile phone. His body seemed to exist in a perpetual state of readiness for danger, a hypervigilance that meant he was constantly scanning his surroundings, particularly in public spaces, always looking for exits, always tracking who was behind him. This constant alertness was exhausting, leaving him drained even before his workday began. His physical reactivity was striking; the distant wail of a siren or the sight of flashing blue lights in his rearview mirror would send his heart racing, his palms sweating, and a wave of nausea washing over him, replicating the terror he had felt that night.

This heightened state of physical and emotional threat, David found, made him acutely vulnerable to his memories of the event. When his system was already primed and on edge, his body taut with hypervigilance, even the most fleeting reminder could plunge him into an overwhelming emotional experience. He would be in the middle of drafting lesson plans, a task that demanded precise focus, when a sudden noise from the street or an authoritative tone from a manager would trigger an intense wave of dread. He often experienced the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or conscious memory, a sudden, debilitating panic that left him shaken and disoriented. These moments were not just fleeting thoughts; they were full-body sensations that felt as real and terrifying as the original event, and when they hit, he would feel so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes needing to retreat to the quiet of his office bathroom to regain composure. He struggled to articulate the specifics of what had happened, often saying, "I can't seem to put the frightening event into words," despite the vividness of his internal emotional landscape.

The cumulative effect of these experiences had begun to erode David's professional and personal life. His ability to concentrate on his curriculum design work, which required sustained mental effort, had suffered significantly, leading to missed deadlines and increased stress. At home, his wife, though supportive, struggled to understand why he was always on edge, why he flinched at her touch, or why he insisted on checking the locks multiple times each night. He felt increasingly isolated, burdened by memories that felt both intensely present and stubbornly ineffable. David finally sought help, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant alarm bells ringing within him and reclaim a sense of peace that had been absent for far too long. He was most afraid that this constant state of terror would define the rest of his life, permanently altering the man he once was.
